newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai controls on baht effective - Pacific Asset.
newsitem.headline: Thai controls on baht effective - Pacific Asset.

text.p: The Bank of Thailand's recently imposed capital controls are effective in countering speculative attacks on the baht and are not necessarily costly as labelled by some, a Singapore-based fixed income fund manager said.

"Capital controls do not cost Thailand much, if anything. They could be maintained for years with net positive effect for both investor and central bank. The speculators are finished if the (Bank of Thailand) continues on this track," said an executive of Pacific Asset Management in a report released on Monday.

"In fact, the controls put in place by the Bank of Thailand will probably prove to be quite easy to live with. After all, they are not much different from those utilised by some of the fastest growing Asian tigers over the past four decades," said David Carbon, partner and market strategist at the firm.
The baht was heavily attacked last month by offshore players who believed the central bank might soon devalue the currency or widen the baht band that would cause the baht's value to fall.
The central bank struck back by cutting supplies of the baht to foreign speculators, forcing them to acquire it to cover short positions at exorbitant rates.
The squeeze is still in place and is expected to last another few weeks, analysts said.

The central bank's move created a two-tier market in which spot baht in the offshore market were eight to nine percent higher than in the local market, reflecting the fact that some speculators were still trying to unwind their short positions.

Some analysts said the capital controls should be dismantled because these measures were more costly than the problems they were designed to solve as they could cut off capital inflows needed to finance the current account deficit and hit growth. Carbon, however, argued that was not necessarily the case.

"In the first place, the (central bank) has instituted controls on capital outflow, not inflow. Direct and portfolio investment is still free to enter the country, and to exit as and when the investor desires," he said in the report.
"The truth is, capital controls in Thailand are not a tourniquet twisted around some gushing imbalance in the economy." he said.

"Their task is a simple and eminently reasonable one: to prevent speculators from borrowing baht, which should allow the authorities to lower interest rates a modest two to three percent. With moderate goals like these, controls can exist for a long time and be very effective," he added.
